entries.title: New Report Reveals How Much Investors in Trump’s Crypto Ventures Have Lost
entries.summary: The president’s expanding crypto empire has vastly increased his overall wealth. His investors, not so much.
entries.content:
Investors in President Donald Trump’s family crypto business have lost an estimated $4.7 billion, according to an analysis released Thursday by consumer advocacy watchdog Public Citizen.

The report examined five products: non-fungible tokens of Trump Digital Trading Cards; a meme coin that launched days before Trump’s inauguration; a governance token of World Liberty Financial, the stablecoin and trading platform co-founded by Trump and his three sons; a digital dollar stablecoin launched by WLF; and Trump Media’s digital-asset treasury.

Trump’s family is building an expanding crypto empire that has vastly increased the president’s overall wealth. Trump earned more than $1.1 billion from cryptocurrency in 2025, according to an annual financial disclosure released in June.

The majority of investor losses — roughly $3.2 billion, largely in unrealized losses — appeared to come from the Trump meme coin that decreased in value, according to Public Citizen.

“The earliest buyers were positioned for extraordinary gains; the far larger waves that bought during and after the surge were left holding tokens now worth a fraction of what they paid,” the report says.

Public Citizen estimated that WLF’s governance token cost investors nearly $1 billion in losses, followed by paper losses of roughly $450 million from Trump Media’s bitcoin business. The digital trading cards were estimated to have lost investors at least $9.3 million, and the dollar stablecoin has no projected losses, according to the report.

The White House and World Liberty Financial did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Public Citizen’s report.

White House counsel David Warrington has previously said that Trump has “no involvement in business deals that would implicate his constitutional responsibilities.” The White House has also maintained that Trump has no conflicts of interests.

Trump and his family launched WFL in September 2024 before quietly selling a 49% stake to a group backed by an Abu Dhabi royal. WFL has continued to financially benefit the Trump family through a complicated legal structure.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez

entries.title: Bovino Says DHS Wants Him Dead. The White House Says That’s 'Absurd.'
entries.summary: It’s the latest instance of the administration attempting to distance itself from the former Border Patrol chief.
entries.content:
Former senior Border Patrol official Gregory Bovino said the Trump administration “absolutely” wants him killed after taking away his security detail earlier this year, a claim the White House called “absurd.”

“Do I think they want me dead at this point? Yes.” Bovino told conservative media personality and podcaster Tucker Carlson. “I'm in a running battle every time I go out. … There's some crazies out there.”

Since Bovino announced his retirement in March — which may not have been entirely voluntary, according to Bovino’s exit interview with The New York Times — the former top immigration official has openly criticized high-profile members of the Trump administration including White House border czar Tom Homan.

Bovnio told Carlson that U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s commissioner, Rodney Scott, pulled his security detail while Homan was present and said it was done in an effort to “silence” him. It was not clear when Bovino had a security detail or when it ended.

“This is absurd,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis wrote in a statement. “Tom Homan is an American patriot and career law enforcement officer with decades of experience effectively protecting American communities and deporting illegal aliens.”

Bovino quickly rose to prominence in President Donald Trump's second term, with then- Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem referring to him as “Border Patrol Commander at Large” in an October 2025 op-ed in The Wall Street Journal.

Bovino led the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration-enforcement crackdown in Minnesota called Operation Metro Surge, but he was demoted in January after federal agents shot and killed U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

Homan took over and ended the large-scale enforcement efforts in Minnesota, while Bovino was reassigned to his previous role as chief agent of the Border Patrol's El Centro Sector in California. He then retired.

Since leaving his post in the Trump administration, Bovino has been critical of his former Homeland Security colleagues’ immigration-enforcement efforts.

When Carlson asked about the current state of illegal immigration, Bovino said “one word comes to mind, that’s catastrophe.”

“They want you to think mass deportations are happening. They’re not. It’s theater,” Bovino wrote in a post on X with the video of his appearance on Carlson’s podcast.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Hegseth Is Weighing a Controversial Pentagon Spokesperson for the Army’s Top Job
entries.summary: Sean Parnell’s confirmation could face a rocky path in the Senate because of his partisan profile and past abuse allegations.
entries.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth favors Sean Parnell to become the next Army secretary, according to two former Pentagon officials, but the Pentagon spokesperson would probably face a tough path to Senate confirmation.

Hegseth is considering Parnell to succeed Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who is reportedly weighing a departure from the Pentagon in the coming weeks. The former officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations, confirmed a report in The Hill that Parnell is short-listed for the role.

Parnell is a decorated Afghanistan veteran, former congressional candidate and trusted Hegseth adviser, but his partisan political profile, combative posture toward the press and past domestic abuse allegations — which he denies — could complicate any confirmation effort.

“It would be a difficult confirmation process, and you’d have to want to volunteer to have that all gone through in the public,” a third former Pentagon official said. “You’re going to revisit all of that.”

Although Parnell could face a confirmation fight, President Donald Trump could skirt the issue by designating him as the acting secretary. Under the Federal Vacancies Act, Parnell could serve for 210 days from when the job became vacant, but he could not serve as acting secretary if Trump nominated him for the permanent job.

Army Undersecretary Mike Obadal and Army Comptroller Marc Andersen have also surfaced as possible successors. Obadal, a respected former special operations officer who worked as a defense industry executive before joining the Trump administration last year, does not appear to be campaigning to become secretary, one of the former officials said. Obadal declined to comment.

Obadal would face his own confirmation hurdle. Federal law bars anyone from serving as Army secretary within five years of leaving active duty, but Obadal exited the military in 2022, so he would need Congress to approve a waiver.

Andersen, the assistant secretary of the Army for financial management, is less well known outside the Pentagon and on Capitol Hill, which makes any potential confirmation dynamics tough to predict.

Parnell floated his own name in the past year, according to one of the former officials. In response to a request to the Pentagon for comment, however, a senior administration official provided a brief statement: “Sean Parnell is 100% focused on the job he was appointed to by President Trump and Secretary Hegseth.”

The deliberations come as Driscoll considers leaving the administration after a monthslong struggle with Hegseth. Media reports suggest he could depart soon — one of the former officials said it could be around Labor Day — though his exit date would hinge on White House approval.

Parnell has served as the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson for most of President Donald Trump’s second term and is a senior adviser to Hegseth. He also chairs the administration’s review of the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan.

The former officials said Parnell would face significant resistance in the Senate. Some Republicans could be reluctant to support him, and his prospects would worsen sharply if Democrats win control of the chamber in the November midterms.

Critics say Parnell is highly partisan and too closely aligned with Hegseth. One former official pointed to Parnell’s adversarial posture toward members of the media and criticism that the Afghanistan review he is leading is one-sided.

Parnell twice sought federal office in Pennsylvania. He lost a 2020 House race to Democrat Conor Lamb andwithdrew from the 2022 Republican Senate primary after losing a child-custody fight. During divorce proceedings, Parnell’s estranged wife alleged she endured years of rage and abuse from him, including being choked — charges he called “baseless” at the time.

Otherwise, Obadal, the Army’s Senate-confirmed No. 2 civilian official, would typically be in line to perform the secretary’s duties if Driscoll leaves.

Correction: An earlier version of this story incorrectly described Sean Parnell's eligibility to be named acting secretary. He could serve in that role temporarily under the Federal Vacancies Act.
entries.author: Joe Gould

entries.title: Trump Is Actually Going Through With His ‘Lake America’ Name Change
entries.summary: “We have a Gulf, and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean,” he said, floating another name change for the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump on Thursday signed an executive order meant to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America,” taking his apparent jab at Canada one step further as a trade war between the two countries escalates.

The president said the name change was “effective immediately” during a signing ceremony in the Oval Office. The executive order directs Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to update the Geographic Names Information Service to reflect the name change.

When asked by reporters about the move, Trump said he was sending “no message” to Canada with the name change.

“Lake of America was something I've been thinking about for a long time,” the president said. “Actually, as you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it, and now it's very routinely the Gulf of America.”

“If you think about it, we have a Gulf, and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean,” Trump added, floating a potential name change for the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean.

The executive order argues that because more of the lake’s volume lies within territory claimed by the United States, Trump has the right to unilaterally change its name. 

The name change came two days after Trump had threatened to do so in a Truth Social post, explicitly connecting the move to trade negotiations between the U.S. and Canada that flamed out at the last minute Friday night.

The U.S. and Canada have been entrenched in a trade war since Trump imposed tariffs on America’s northern neighbor in early 2025. In February, the Supreme Court struck down the sweeping international duties that the president levied through a string of executive orders.

But tensions between the trading partners escalated earlier this month when Trump threatened new tariffs of up to 50% on $20 billion in Canadian goods. Canada retaliated with its own sweeping tariffs — further complicating the relationship between the two countries that exchanged more than $870 billion in annual trade in 2025.

While Trump can unilaterally call the lake a new name, it doesn’t mean other countries, or even localities within the United States, have to abide by it.

A defiant New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said on X that her state state, which borders the lake, would not follow Trump’s instruction to change the lake’s name.

After Trump’s announcement, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pointed out that the name predates both the U.S. and Canada. “Ontario” comes from the Wendat indigenous word meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”

The Interior Department’s U.S. Geological Survey is the lead agency that handles renaming requests, and Trump’s speedy renaming of the Gulf of Mexico sent the agency into disarray, as NOTUS previously reported.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum continued to call it the Gulf of Mexico, despite Trump’s push to relabel the body of water.

There was also significant bipartisan pushback from Alaska politicians against Trump’s order to rename Mount Denali in Alaska to Mount McKinley. President Barack Obama’s administration changed the name in 2015 to honor Alaskan native groups’ original name for the peak — which translates to “the tall one” — after a decades-long campaign by the state. In 1896, the mountain was named for William McKinley, the 25th U.S. president, who never visited the state.

In the executive order announcing the mountain's name change, the White House described the move as an effort to restore “names that honor American greatness.”

This story has been updated with further information.
entries.author: Jackie Llanos, Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Jon Ossoff Assails GOP Rival After Report Reveals Former Staffer’s Nazi Posts
entries.summary: He said Rep. Mike Collins’ judgement in hiring was “unacceptable and disqualifying.”
entries.content:
Sen. Jon Ossoff assailed his Republican rival, Rep. Mike Collins, on Thursday following a report that the congressman’s office had formerly employed a staffer with a history of racist posts online, including Nazi and KKK imagery.

Ossoff, a Democrat running for reelection in Georgia against the embattled Collins, made the comments in a press conference initially meant to focus on an ongoing probe into Collins’ use of taxpayer dollars being conducted by the House Ethics Committee.

That was before The Washington Post published a bombshell report Thursday morning detailing a number of posts made by Preston Parra, a former intern for Collins and a contractor for his leadership PAC. He reportedly posted on X a picture of himself wearing a Klu Klux Klan robe, another of a swastika made up of the word “twink,” and used the phrase “white power” several times.

Ossoff said that hiring Parra was evidence of Collins’ ties to white nationalism and neo-Nazi ideology. He also cited reports about the House member’s son-in-law, who is a pro-white nationalist social media influencer, and his then-chief of staff using his position to help a jailed Holocaust denier.

“This morning's news should shock not just the entire state of Georgia but the entire country,” Ossoff said. “Yet more evidence of a sitting congressman's extensive ties to white nationalism and neo-Nazi ideology. This time, it's swastikas and the costume of the Ku Klux Klan, unacceptable and disqualifying.”

“It is the year 2026 in the state of Georgia, it's not 1935, it's not 1958,” Ossoff added.

In response to Parra’s posts, a Collins spokesperson tried to connect Ossoff to left-wing commentator Hasan Piker. Ossoff is one of the Democrats who has condemned Piker for saying American Jews support for Israel could incite violence.

“Preston Parra has no affiliation with Mike Collins’ office or campaign,” Collins spokesperson Meyer Siegfried said in a statement. “The posts are vile, completely unhinged, and Mike Collins unequivocally condemns them.”

Overhaul PAC paid Parra $7,700 for fundraising consulting in May 2025, according to Federal Election Commission records. In an interview with the Post, Parra said he considered himself a provocateur and not a white supremacist.

Parra has continued to double down on his rhetoric on social media, referring to a reporter with a racial slur.
entries.author: Jackie Llanos

entries.title: USPS Says Trump’s New Policies for Mail-In Voting Are In Effect
entries.summary: The Postal Service acknowledged the “pending litigation” on the final rule.
entries.content:
The U.S. Postal Service announced Thursday that the Trump administration's requirements for mail-in voting are now in force while courts hear challenges to the president’s crackdown on the practice ahead of the midterm elections.

USPS said in an FAQ that the new rule is now in effect after a Supreme Court ruling lifted several court actions blocking the policy this week. Under the rule, the Postal Service will be charged with comparing ballots to an eligible list of voters created by the Trump administration through states submitting their voter rolls.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March that sought to reshape the federal government’s role in the election process, including by cracking down on voting by mail. States have the constitutional authority to administer elections, but the president has attempted to take some control of the process.

Trump’s policy mandates spurred legal challenges from 23 states and the District of Columbia.

After the Supreme Court lifted the injunction barring the policy from taking effect, the almost two dozen states refiled their legal challenge to the rule. The high court’s ruling, which supersedes any other precedent, also delivered a win for the Trump administration by lifting the injunction in a separate federal lawsuit led by several voting rights groups.

USPS acknowledged the “pending litigation” on the final rule and committed to updating the FAQ “as necessary.”
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Wife of USS Lincoln Sailor Says He’s Facing Discipline for Apparent Suicide Attempt
entries.summary: The wife of a Navy sailor aboard the beleaguered aircraft carrier said the service member was accused of two violations of the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
entries.content:
A Navy sailor who jumped overboard in an apparent suicide attempt while serving aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln is facing disciplinary action, the service member’s wife told MS NOW Wednesday.

The wife, who spoke to the outlet on the condition of anonymity, said the service member was accused of violating two articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice. The sailor jumped overboard on Aug. 3 and had been repeatedly denied requests for paternity leave, his wife said.

Charging documents reviewed by MS NOW claimed the 19-year-old sailor violated Article 83 for “malingering” — described as a service member inflicting self-injury or faking a physical or mental illness to skirt military duties — as well as Article 86 for “absence without leave.”

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

Public outcry surged this month after reports circulated about deteriorating conditions and low morale aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln during its record-breaking deployment. The aircraft carrier, which has been supporting military operations in Iran, left its home port in San Diego in November 2025. The deployment has since broken the record for most consecutive days at sea without a port call.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has denied allegations of dire living conditions aboard the Lincoln, telling reporters that such claims were “completely misrepresented.”

“We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” Hegseth said during a trip to Panama earlier this month. “Some deployments are longer than others, and ⁠I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody.”

The USS George Washington was dispatched to replace the Lincoln shortly after demands for answers grew. The Lincoln will make a port call in Thailand next week before heading to its home base in the U.S., according to The Associated Press.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez

entries.title: GOP Governor Says Biden Considered Pardoning Trump in 2023
entries.summary: Spencer Cox, a Republican, made the surprising revelation in a new book set for release next month.
entries.content:
Gov. Spencer Cox of Utah is going public with private conversations he held with then-President Joe Biden in 2023, saying he tried to persuade Biden to pardon Donald Trump on the criminal charges he faced in multiple jurisdictions.

Surprisingly, he recalled, Biden seemed open to the idea.

Cox said he spoke with Biden about pardoning Trump as the pair sat in the presidential limousine driving through Salt Lake City.

“You know, I’ve actually considered this for a while,” Biden reportedly replied to Cox. “In fact, just this week as we were lying in bed, Jill and I had a long conversation about it.”

Cox’s anecdote is included in a new book, obtained by The Atlantic ahead of its scheduled release next month, titled, “Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt.”

The iconoclastic Republican governor, who has attempted to brand himself as a bipartisan figure willing to work across the aisle, said the request was made as part of a bid to unite a divided country.

The pardon never came, but Cox believed an olive branch from Biden to Trump could have curbed some of the deepening partisan tensions between the parties.

The governor has spent years focusing on initiatives to address partisan polarization and harmful rhetoric — writing in his book that his “research became painfully pertinent” after the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk while he was speaking at a Utah university in September 2025.

Cox did not vote for Trump in 2016 or 2020, but he eventually changed his tune and backed Trump after the assassination attempt against the president at the rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, in 2024. The governor told The Atlantic that his decision spurred backlash “much stronger than I expected.”

“You have the opportunity to do something that no other person on earth can do right now: unify and save our country,” Cox wrote in a letter to Trump, expressing his support.

In Cox’s new book, he said that neither experience with the two presidents turned out “quite the way I’d hoped.”

“When I spoke with President Biden, I hoped he would choose mercy over escalation,” the governor wrote. “When I wrote to President Trump, I hoped he would choose unity over retaliation.”

Cox launched Disagree Better when he was chair of the National Governors Association in 2023, seeking to “reduce inflammatory rhetoric and foster a culture of healthy debate.” The initiative is now an independent nonprofit and remains one Cox’s chief efforts to fight harmful political partisanship — a pursuit he catalogues in his book.

“At some point we have to find an off-ramp, or it’s going to get much, much worse,” Cox said in an address days after Kirk’s assassination.

A few months later, Cox traveled with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, to make the case in Washington, D.C., that political leaders needed to dial back their rhetoric, including Trump.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Former Stars and Stripes Journalists Sue Pete Hegseth After Firings
entries.summary: The journalists argue they were let go “for speaking up as private citizens in support of the press’s freedom.”
entries.content:
Three former Stars and Stripes journalists sued Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and agency spokesperson Sean Parnell on Thursday, claiming the Trump administration pursued "extraordinary censorship efforts" against the news outlet and illegally fired them.

The Pentagon fired three journalists — Publisher Max Lederer, Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin and reporter Lara Korte — on Aug. 21 for insubordination. The purge violated their First Amendment rights, the lawsuit alleges.

Korte wrote in a Thursday post on X that “everyone deserves the right to a free and independent press, especially our service members.”

“This lawsuit is about safeguarding the mission of Stars and Stripes journalists so they can continue to do their jobs without fear or retaliation,” she said.

The Department of Defense did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Slavin and Korte said their firing for insubordination was related to interviews they gave during a CBS News segment that aired last month, in which they defended the independence of the partially federally funded paper.

“According to the notice, I am being fired for stating in a CBS interview that hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a personal red line,” Slavin said in a statement to NOTUS last week. “The Pentagon’s public affairs office has charged me with insubordination. I stand by the principle that Stars and Stripes must remain editorially independent, as required by law and by the department’s own policies.”

Over a month after the CBS interviews, Stars and Stripes published a story detailing mental health problems, food and water shortages and other poor conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln. More than five weeks after the story ran, Pentagon officials ordered Lederer to present separation notices to Slavin and Korte, the lawsuit says.

Lederer did not deliver the notices, instead announcing his plans to retire next month over "fundamental" differences with the department after serving as the paper’s publisher for 19 years. The Pentagon fired him before he could retire.

Last April, the Pentagon also fired Jacqueline Smith, the publication’s ombudsman who focused on maintaining the paper’s editorial independence.

The newspaper’s mission had been called into question in January when Parnell called the publication “woke” and said it would return to its original goal of reporting for military members.

“We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members,” Parnell said on X. “Stars & Stripes will be custom tailored to our warfighters. It will focus on warfighting, weapons systems, fitness, lethality, survivability, and ALL THINGS MILITARY. No more repurposed DC gossip columns; no more Associated Press reprints.”
entries.author: Torrie Herrington

entries.title: Wyoming Governor Asks State Attorney General to Investigate DOJ Election Observers
entries.summary: Republican Gov. Mark Gordon called the observers’ conduct during last week’s primary ‘aggressive’ and ‘irregular.’
entries.content:
Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon said he asked the state attorney general to “start looking into” the conduct of Justice Department election observers deployed to the state for last week’s primary election.

“It sounded like the behavior of the observers was a bit aggressive,” Gordon told the state canvassing board on Wednesday, according to NBC News. “It just was irregular, and I have asked the attorney general to start looking into, you know, kind of the nature of the visits and all that sort of stuff.”

The Justice Department sent observers to Wyoming as part of a broad effort by President Donald Trump’s administration to override states’ authority to administer and monitor elections. The president has continued to allege that there has been widespread fraud in elections and has pushed to increase federal control over the voting process.

Two attorneys from the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division monitored polls in Laramie County, according to a press release posted last week.

Gordon, a Republican, noted that while he did not oppose the election observers’ presence, he believes their “behavior seemed to exceed what the authority that Congress had given them was.”

Laramie County Clerk Debra Lee said the observers asked questions that were “outside the scope of federal voting rights laws,” and asked to interview voters before Lee blocked their requests.

The Republican election official also railed against the attorneys’ deployment in the county, calling it “a poorly managed exercise and one that showed complete disregard for our state laws and administration of our elections.”

The Wyoming attorney general’s office did not respond to a request for comment. It remains unclear whether state authorities will further investigate the issues.

The DOJ announced it was sending election monitors to Wyoming and Florida on the same day of their primaries. Gordon said state and local election officials like Lee were not aware of their arrival.

“Shortly after learning of their presence, I spoke with a DOJ official in Washington who informed me that the decision to deploy monitors to Wyoming was made on short notice, and an email had been sent to me, but it may have gone to the wrong address,” Lee said in a statement to NBC News.

Harmeet K. Dhillon, the DOJ’s assistant attorney general of the Civil Rights Division, has led the mobilization of federal election monitors to states across the country — sending 75 monitors across five states and over 200 polling locations this primary season.

“Election monitoring is an ongoing priority for this office,” Dhillon wrote in its announcement last week.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin
